	  fmt = @battler.actor? ? Vocab::ActorDrain : Vocab::EnemyDrain
	  sprintf(fmt, @battler.name, @hp_drain, Vocab::hp)

	  sprintf(fmt, @battler.name)
	end
  end
  #--------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # * Get Text for MP Damage
  #--------------------------------------------------------------------------

	if @mp_drain > 0
	  fmt = @battler.actor? ? Vocab::ActorDrain : Vocab::EnemyDrain
	  sprintf(fmt, @battler.name, @mp_drain, Vocab::mp)
	elsif @mp_damage > 0
	  fmt = @battler.actor? ? Vocab::ActorLoss : Vocab::EnemyLoss
	  sprintf(fmt, @battler.name, @mp_damage, Vocab::mp)
	elsif @mp_damage < 0

	  sprintf(fmt, @battler.name, -@mp_damage, Vocab::mp)
	else

	end
  end

posts.author: BigEd781
posts.body:
Onkei69 said:
I was wondering, when should I define a module rather than a class ?
Are there drawbacks in using modules ?
Click to expand...
So, modules have two major uses:
1. They act as a namespace, i.e., a way to group methods and constants to avoid naming clashes.  This is typically how modules are used in RM scripts.
2. The implement mixin functionality.  I almost never see this used in the context of RPG Maker, but it is great for larger systems.
In case you unfamiliar with the concept of a mixin, here is an article that explains it in more depth than I would here.  It is an alternative to inheritance (side not: inheritance is often used incorrectly as a way to use methods from one class in another class.  This is not the intent of inheritance.)
http://juixe.com/tec...mixins-in-ruby/

posts.author: Yato
posts.body:
@Kaelan: There is not a variant by default, but it's easy enough to make.
Spoiler
Code:
class Window_Base < Window
  #--------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # * Draw Character Graphic
  #--------------------------------------------------------------------------
  def draw_character(character_name, character_index, x, y, d = 0)
	return unless character_name
	bitmap = Cache.character(character_name)
	sign = character_name[/^[\!\$]./]
	if sign && sign.include?('$')
	  cw = bitmap.width / 3
	  ch = bitmap.height / 4
	else
	  cw = bitmap.width / 12
	  ch = bitmap.height / 8
	end
	n = character_index
	src_rect = Rect.new((n%4*3+1)*cw, (n/4*4+d)*ch, cw, ch)
	contents.blt(x - cw / 2, y - ch, bitmap, src_rect)
  end
  #--------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # * Draw Actor Walking Graphic
  #--------------------------------------------------------------------------
  def draw_actor_graphic(actor, x, y, direction = 0)
	draw_character(actor.character_name, actor.character_index, x, y, direction)
  end
end
Just use draw_actor_graphic(actor, x, y, dir) where dir is
0 - Down
1 - Left
2 - Right
3 - Up
You can leave out the dir if you want the sprite facing down

ex: "if RGSS.version == 3"

posts.author: Solistra
posts.body:
You'd have to look at Game.ini and read which DLL will be used for the game, which is entirely possible. This is also probably a wildly inefficient hack, but this will check in Game.ini for the RGSS version and return the more usable "RGSS1", "RGSS2", or "RGSS3" that you might be expecting.
Code:
file = File.open("Game.ini")
file.each { |line|
  @version = line.match(/RGSS[1,2,3]/)[0] if line.match(/^Library=/)
}
Edit:
Replaced my original post, which was interesting, but not thought out well enough for my tastes. This works far better than what I originally posted anyway.

Question(s) of the day...
What is a Fiber and how can i yield one ?
Click to expand...
I know Tsukihime already answered this, but I thought that the answer could use some more explanation. Fibers are... relatively obscure, honestly, but what they do is essentially store code to be run that can be passed back and forth from the Fiber to whatever called it. When you create a new instance of the Fiber class, you pass it code to run -- usually in the form of a block, but not always. Once the Fiber is created, it does... absolutely nothing. In order to get the Fiber to do anything, you have to call the resume method on it, which will begin running the Fiber from the beginning of the code block passed to it. From there, the Fiber will continue to run this code until the end of the code block or until a call is made to Fiber.yield. When you call that, control is passed back to the caller of the Fiber until the resume method is called on the Fiber once more, at which point it picks back up where it left off (and the cycle continues).
In VX Ace, Fibers are used in Game_Interpreter and Window_Message to control when code is run, basically. Each Game_Interpreter has its own fiber that is used to control when its code is to be executed (pausing it under a number of circumstances, such as screen changes or when the message window is processing). Window_Message uses it similarly, but mainly to control when text processing is done.
Honestly, though, there's very little need for much of anyone scripting for RPG Maker to make use of Fibers. Why the interest in them, if I may ask?

Events in a map are only available when that map is loaded. You would either have to load the map into a temporary variable (NOT $game_map, but you could do it the same way the Game_Map class loads its map data), or you would have to know what events exist on each map.

class Game_Interpreter  def example(mapid)    events = load_data(sprintf("Data/Map%03d.rvdata2", mapid)).events.keys    for eventid in events      $game_self_switches[[mapid, eventid, 'A']] = false    end  endendYou may also need to add a check - if mapid happens to be the id of the currently loaded map, you might need to add a $game_map.need_refresh = true after updating all the events.

posts.body:
You also should not trust the FPS display as a means of actual benchmarking as it is not 100% accurate. An FPS drop can also be caused by a number of different things not directly in your control (eg., garbage collection). If you are noticing some actual visual stutter, then it might be worth it to benchmark and find your bottleneck.
Drawing text is indeed slow. My script alleviates some of this by adding the cache, but you may have noticed adds a tremendous amount of overhead to each draw_text command (while actually accessing the underlying method less), as well as individually having to calculate where to draw each letter. Net result, the longer the string being drawn, the less of an improvement you will see due to this calculation (the actual draw is much faster since its just a simple blt instead of accessing the font and asking it it to build a letter, but the letter iteration and calculating of the position is much slower). On the flipside, the normal overhead the draw_text method has to go through just to access the font is also slow, so you will see a tremendous improvement on smaller strings.
That was a bit of a tangent but the point I am getting at is if you want to see improvement, you need to identify your bottleneck and either solve it by replacing it completely with a more efficient method, write around it in such a way that you have to access it less (as above), or find a better time or times to access the method (eg., my Window Selectable MAX VX script (
http://pastebin.com/xHptRXKs
) where I only drew the visible areas of any scrolling Window_Selectable window and drew a limited number of items per frame). For example, if you have indeed determined drawing rects is too slow for you, you could either write a completely new method to draw rects, try using a different operation like blt so you only have to draw them once (if the pages are static, you could also consider saving the entire bitmap instead of redrawing it as lemony suggested), or draw them when it wont be a drag on your framerate.

@dekita
Yeah, my script also does a staggered draw ahead of what is displayed so that you'll never have more load than the initial displayed area being drawn. To your other question and to add to Tsukihime,
Using the & symbol in front of a variable at the end of your argument list binds it to a variable that you can then pass around as a proc. If you use the & when passing this back as an argument into a method, it is read as a block. You can mix and match these behaviors, much in the same way you can use the splat (*) to collect arguments into an array or expand them into an argument list. If you don't explicitly bind it into a variable, the block at the end of an argument list is still implicitly passed and can be accessed using yield.
Ruby will pass a given block automatically if it is tacked onto the end of a method, however, this does not happen when a method has been aliased and at some point has the aliased method called within it - if a block was given there, it would need to be explicitly passed, so they then bind it to the variable and pass it transparently, as with the argument list. I suspect may scripters do this because with the way Rpg Maker scripts are and with the possibility of having so many different chefs in the kitchen, so to speak, it is impossible to know what a method will actually do. This encompasses nearly every usage I have seen for the practice of binding a block in RPG maker scripts. However, I find this thinking to be slightly flawed as if the method was changed so drastically as to require a block to function when it did not before, simply transparently passing the block in whatever code you are adding on is probably not going to have the desired result. Its not really making any notable impact either way in this situation, so use your own discretion.

I'll do this line by line using your literal examples.
$my_array = my_class.newYou've initialized a new object called $my_array, but is it really an array? Unless 'my_class' is a child class of Array or has operator methods that simulate an array, $my_array is
not
an array object.
$my_array += my_class.newLet's assume $my_array is really an Array object ( '
$my_array = []
' ). In this case, this statement will not work and you'll receive an error. The '+' operator for array objects only concatenates other array objects.
Example link here.
$my_array[1] = my_class.newAgain, assume $my_array is an actual Array object ( '
$my_array = []
' ). In this case, you won't receive an error since you are instantiating an object into a specified element. But you've essentially created this array:
$my_array[1] = my_class.new    # => [nil, my_class.new]You must remember that Ruby (and practically every other programming language) uses zero-based numbering:
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-based_numbering
This means the first element of an array is at index 0, the second element is at index 1, etc.
So to answer your question, what's the difference between the two ways? One doesn't work, and the other does (but probably not in the way that you want).
Let's rewrite your examples in another way.
$my_array = []This statement initializes '$my_array' into an empty array. This eliminates any ambiguity in regards to what kind of object '
$my_array
' is.
'
$my_array = Array.new
' is an equivalent statement, by the way.
$my_array = []       # => []$my_array.push(1)    # => [1]$my_array.push(2)    # => [1, 2]$my_array.push(3)    # => [1, 2, 3]$my_array[1]         # => 2For learning purposes, use '
push
' to add new objects into an array. '
push
' will guarantee that the object you add will be placed after the last element in the array. '
$my_array.push(obj)
' is equivalent to '
$my_array[$my_array.size] = obj
'
Also, most any programmer understands the basic concept of a stack (first in, last out). So whenever anyone else looks at your code and sees '
push
', they will know at a glance that $my_array is an Array object without even looking at what $my_array was initialized as.
The opposite of '
push
' is '
pop
'.
$my_array = [1, 2, 3]$my_array.pop            # => 3$my_array                # => [1, 2]
And using your 'my_class' object:
$my_array = []foo = My_class.new$my_array.push(foo)$my_array # => [foo]
Edit: I just remembered. The first letter of a class name in Ruby must be capitalized. (e.g. class My_class)

What is the difference between x/y, self.x/self.y and @x/@y in a class?In Sprite_Character, the update_position method does this:

Click to expand...
Short answer is that in the case of Sprite objects, the assignment operators for x= and y= store value in the metadata rather than in an instance variable. You can't access them with @x and @y unless other methods have been added to allow this. If there are no redefinitions for x and y, try looking for attr_reader methods, as these would also change the default functionality. Try looking in every superclass. The metadata for Sprite wont allow nil assignment for x or y, so something has to be changing the accessors for either to be read as nil on the move_animation line.self.x refers to the method 'x' for the object at the current scope. 'x' refers to the local variable x, or, if it does not exist, the method 'x' at the current scope. @x refers to the instance variable @x. In many cases, they may refer to the same thing, but they can at times be very different.
To go a bit more in depth, self.x does not necessarily refer to the instance variable @x. If it is a simple attribute reader or accessor method, it will return the value in @x, but otherwise it would work like any other method. As to the variable 'x', this is nearly identical to referencing 'self.x' in
most
situations, including the one you have posted. However, if you attempt to assign something to 'x', you'd be creating a new local variable and not using the assignment operator for the object. So 'x' does not necessarily refer to the same value 'self.x' or '@x'. 'self.x =' does not necessarily assign a value to @x (in the case of Sprite, it does not), and using a 'x =' will never assign the value to @x as it will assign to the local variable x (you need to explicitly state the object when using an assignment operator, which is why the 'self' on those lines).
In the case you have posted above, you should always use the accessor methods. Sprites use their metadata to determine where they should be displayed on screen, they wont recognize values that are just put into instance variables. That just leaves the matter of what redefined the reader method, and why.. and I can't think of anything off the top of my head here as to why that would be done.
In other situations, I still prefer to use the methods even if they are simple accessors. Sure, just referencing the instance variable directly saves a modicum of processor time, but it is a lot easier to deal with changing situations if you always use accessors, because you can alias or redefine the accessors. Having the methods encapsulated like this gives you much more control over the data in the event you need to change something. I don't feel that it is necessary to always explicitly access the variables using 'self' (except, of course, when performing assignment), but this is a personal preference. For example, if you
ever
use x as a local variable within the same class, you should probably denote when you are using the accesssor method by using self.x. Of course, if you are only using the variables locally but across many methods, a simple instance variable will do the trick without the need for any accessors

Unfortunately, just using the code as presented in the interpreter doesn't work. I tried this a while ago and had to resort to something a bit uglier.
This did the trick for me, but someone else might be able to make a nicer one:
Code:
#--------------------------------------------------------------------------  # * Jump to Label  #--------------------------------------------------------------------------  def command_119    # Shaz - @temp_label is used for a dynamic label    label_name = @temp_label.nil? ? @params[0] : @temp_label    @temp_label = nil    @list.size.times do |i|      if @list[i].code == 118 && @list[i].parameters[0] == label_name        @index = i        return      end    end  end
Then in your event code:
Code:
Script: @temp_label = "label" + $game_variables[1].to_sJump to Label: xxxLabel: label1...Label: label2...Label: label3
The Jump to Label: xxx can be anything - if @temp_label has been populated, whatever you put in here will be ignored and whatever you set in the script call will be the label used. Make sure, if the Script call goes over 2 lines, that the break is in the correct place (after the + is a good spot).
